papers.title_en: Code-as-Auditor: Executable Compliance Reasoning via Regulation-to-Code
papers.authors: Jisoo Kim, Taeyoon Kwack, Jinwoo Jang, Woo Kyung Kim, Honguk Woo
papers.evidence: 用于合规推理的可解释代码结构和决策树
papers.tldr: 针对LLM合规与法律推理缺乏法律逻辑与证据支撑的问题，本文提出Code-as-Auditor：将法规编译为可执行的清单与决策树，并在推理中动态生成正反事实问题与自校验，实现从证据识别到规则应用的可追溯评估；在隐私与数据保护任务上显著提升准确性与可解释性。
papers.abstract_en: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted for compliance and legal reasoning tasks, yet their outputs often lack explicit grounding in legal logic and evidence. We present Code-as-Auditor, an LLM-based framework that extends the model's reasoning capability toward structured and evidence-grounded compliance assessment. The framework translates regulatory information into (1) formalized checklists and executable decision trees, encoding regulations and conditions as interpretable code structures. During inference, each checklist item is (2) dynamically expanded into factual and counterfactual questions, guiding the model to reason over case-specific evidence and potential violations. This process establishes a reasoning pipeline that proceeds from evidence identification, through rule application, to final decision-making, while a self-verification loop improves the logical consistency of the generated code and the traceability of outcomes. Experiments on privacy and data protection scenarios demonstrate that Code-as-Auditor delivers more accurate and evidence-backed evaluations, enabling automated compliance regulation checking grounded in explicit regulatory criteria.

papers.title_en: Why Some Strikes Last Longer: The Resilience Paradox of Partially Functional Institutions
papers.evidence: 劳工罢工与机构对冲突反应的动力学模型
papers.tldr: 论文探讨罢工在机构部分运转下的持久性，构建最小动力学模型耦合参与、回应与功能；解析与数值揭示“韧性悖论”：残余运转可提升稳态参与，并提出罢工-回应敏感度与精确补偿阈值以划分常规与悖论区间。
papers.abstract_en: Labor strikes do not necessarily lead to complete institutional disruption, particularly when non-striking sectors maintain part of normal activities. We propose a minimal dynamical model to investigate how such residual activity affects the persistence of labor conflicts. The model couples strike participation, institutional response, and overall functionality through two competing mechanisms: a direct suppressive effect of residual activity on strike participation and an indirect effect arising from the reduced institutional pressure to resolve the conflict. Analytical calculations reveal a counterintuitive regime in which increasing residual activity increases, rather than decreases, stationary strike participation. We characterize this behavior through a strike-response susceptibility and derive an exact compensation threshold separating the conventional regime from a resilience-paradox regime. At the threshold, the two mechanisms exactly balance, making stationary strike participation independent of residual activity. Numerical results confirm the analytical predictions and illustrate the underlying mechanism. Our results show that institutional resilience can have an unintended dynamical consequence: by absorbing part of the disruption generated by a strike, continued operation may reduce the urgency of institutional response and thereby favor conflict persistence. This provides a simple example of how individually stabilizing processes can collectively generate counterintuitive outcomes in complex social systems.
